name: Burundi
headline: Burundi passed its first data protection law in March 2026, but its regulator is not yet running and hospital records stay in separate systems.

access.summary: Since March 2026, Law 1/03 gives a free copy of your data within one month, but medical information goes only through a doctor you name. No national patient portal was found, and the data regulator does not exist yet, so the score sits at 40.
detail: Articles 24 and 25 of Law 1/03 of 10 March 2026 give a right to confirmation and to a free copy of your personal data. Requests made electronically get an electronic answer. Extra copies can carry a fee set by the Finance Minister.
Article 33 sets a deadline of one month. Article 32 says medical information can be passed to the person only through a doctor the person designates.
Public bodies have one year from entry into force to comply (Article 53). The agency meant to enforce the law was still a draft decree in June 2026.
Health records sit in each hospital's own software. We found no national portal or app where patients can see their record.

control.summary: The 2026 law lets people object and withdraw consent, but there is no opt-out from sharing and no patient-visible access log. A February 2026 health deal commits Burundi to give the US any data access needed to audit facilities.
detail: Law 1/03 lets a person object to processing for legitimate reasons (Article 22) and seek erasure when consent is withdrawn (Article 28). Health data may be processed with express consent or for urgent medical follow-up (Article 10).
Article 10 also lets the minister in charge of civil status lift the ban on sensitive data processing by ordinance, for public interest reasons.
The Ministry's data governance policy logs staff access to hosted systems, but we found no way for a patient to see who opened their file.
Under section 4.2 of the 2026 US MOU, Burundi commits to give the US any data or on-site access needed to audit up to 5% of facilities.

privacy.summary: Health data is a banned category under Law 1/03 unless an exception applies, with 48-hour breach notice to the regulator and fines up to BIF 20 million. The regulator was not yet set up in mid-2026 and no enforcement exists.
detail: Article 9 of Law 1/03 forbids processing health data, with exceptions in Article 10. Sensitive data must get extra safeguards such as encryption, access controls and security audits.
Breaches must be reported to the agency within 48 hours (Article 45) and to people within 96 hours when risk is high (Article 46). Fines for companies run from BIF 1 to 20 million (Article 47).
The agency sits under the ministry in charge of the digital economy, as the Interior Minister told parliament. A decree to set it up was still in draft in June 2026.
Transfers abroad need an adequate level of protection, judged against a country list set by ministerial ordinance (Article 15). We found no published list. The EU's EHDS does not apply to Burundi.

commercial.summary: Anyone can refuse, free of charge, the use of their data for commercial marketing, and unlawful processing of health data carries fines of BIF 0.5 to 5 million. No rules were found on selling de-identified data or on health apps.
detail: Article 23 of Law 1/03 gives a right to object, without cost or reason, to the use of personal data for commercial, charitable or political marketing.

Article 50 fines unlawful processing of health data between BIF 500,000 and 5 million. Companies with over 200 staff, all public bodies and bodies running health research must keep processing registers and name a data protection officer (Articles 36 and 37).
We found no rules on data brokers, consumer health apps or the sale of anonymised health data. Without a working regulator, these protections are untested.

journey.summary: Most public hospitals run their own software, but DHIS2, SIDAinfo and OpenClinic do not talk to each other, according to April 2026 reporting. A US-funded plan sets EMR, lab and pharmacy rollouts; progress against its 2026 targets is not verified.
detail: Enabel said in July 2026 that over 80% of public hospitals are computerised. Its 2023 report named OpenClinic and Quick Soft as the main hospital systems.
Afrique IT News reported in April 2026 that DHIS2, SIDAInfo and OpenClinic coexist without exchanging data. The government aims for a fully interoperable system using HL7 FHIR.
The February 2026 US MOU commits Burundi to SIDAinfo as its EMR in 460 facilities by 2026, Ibipimo in national and regional labs, and eLMIS in 10% of pharmacies by end 2026.
DHIS2 is the national data warehouse for aggregate reporting, with epidemic data sent daily, under the Ministry's data governance policy. Insurance claims links were not found.

clinical.summary: A clinician can see the record held in their own hospital's system, but there is no shared record across providers. The 2019 national e-health plan described referral links to district hospitals only as a pilot in three health centres.
detail: Hospital records live in local systems such as OpenClinic and Quick Soft. The Ministry policy requires each user to log in and limits access to authorised staff.
The national e-health plan PNDIS II described a pilot in three health centres to computerise records and link referrals with the district hospital. Paper registers were still required alongside.
We found no national rule or system that lets a clinician open a patient's record from another facility, even in an emergency.

research.summary: Law 1/03 allows research on health data with the person's consent, and a national ethics committee reviews studies. But Ministry policy lets facility directors approve research sharing, Article 49 fines unjustified objection to research use, and no regulator exists yet, so the score stays at 50.
detail: Article 10(6) of Law 1/03 allows health research on sensitive data when the person consents. Bodies running health research count as major controllers and must do impact assessments (Article 40).
A National Ethics Committee for the protection of human research subjects exists; its members were appointed by presidential decree in June 2019.
The Ministry policy says research data is shared only for a set purpose, with the facility director's approval, and must be aggregated, anonymised or encrypted.

Article 49 fines a person between BIF 50,000 and 500,000, or jails them up to a year, for objecting without legitimate reason to processing for research or statistics. There is no general research opt-out.
We found no public register of data uses and no check on how the consent rule works in practice.

ai.summary: Burundi has no rules for clinical AI. A national AI strategy validated in April 2026 plans health pilots and an AI commission, but it is a plan, not regulation.
detail: The National AI Strategy 2025-2030, validated in April 2026 with UNDP support, plans a National AI Commission and lists health as a priority sector. About fifteen pilot projects are planned, including in health.
The medicines regulator ABREMA lists rules on medicines and medical devices, but we found no guidance on software or AI as a medical device.
In July 2026 an EU-funded Enabel workshop in Bujumbura covered legal and ethical issues of AI in health care. No binding guidance followed that we could find.

news.headline: Burundi validates its first national data governance strategy
news.why: Sets personal data protection as a pillar of how state data is managed.

news.headline: National Assembly unanimously adopts personal data protection bill
news.why: Gives patients their first legal rights over health and other personal data.

news.headline: United States and Burundi sign five-year health cooperation agreement
news.why: The deal shapes national health record systems and US access to health data.

news.headline: Burundi plans an interoperable health information system using HL7 FHIR
news.why: Linking siloed systems is the step needed for a record that follows the patient.
